items.title: Communities Cancel Trunk-or-Treats in Favor of Traditional Trick-or-Treating This Year
items.summary: Some area cities are encouraging a return to traditional trick-or-treating. At last night's Cherryvale City Council Meeting, Acting City Administrator Karen Davis informed the council that the remaining four members on the Community Center board have given their resignations. Because the Community Center traditionally organized the city's annual trunk-or-treat, Davis and the council discussed the feasibility of another organization putting on the event or returning to traditional trick-or-treating. While some including those with the public library expressed a desire for the event to continue, the consensus was to not hold the event this year, as some residents expressed. Independence Chamber of Commerce President Lisa Wilson says Independence will also not be having a trunk-or-treat this year because of the conflict with Neewollah. The Coffeyville Chamber will host its annual Spooktacular event on Thursday, October 15 th .

items.title: When Prosecutorial Discretion Becomes a Commodity
items.summary: When Prosecutorial Discretion Becomes a Commodity Oklahoma history shows why no prosecutor should have the final, unreviewable power to decide when the criminal law will—or will not—be enforced MIAMI, Okla. — Prosecutors need judgment. They decide whether evidence is sufficient, whether witnesses are credible, what charges fit the facts, whether a plea agreement serves justice and whether limited public resources should be spent pursuing a case. But there is another side to prosecutorial discretion that receives far less attention. A prosecutor also possesses the power not to act. The power not to charge. The power to reduce a charge. The power to dismiss. The power to decline a referral. The power to decide that conduct which might ordinarily result in prosecution will go no further. Usually, those decisions are legitimate exercises of professional judgment. But Oklahoma history demonstrates something that should concern every citizen regardless of politics: Discretionary criminal-justice power has value. And anything with value can be corrupted. items.title: When the Racket Gets a License
items.summary: When the Racket Gets a License How Northeast Oklahoma’s old vice economy may have evolved from illegal protection into legal control There is an old American crime story that usually ends the same way. The bootlegger buys a legitimate business. The gambling boss becomes a developer. The fixer becomes a political donor. The man who once needed the sheriff to look the other way learns that it is safer to own the building, hire the lawyer, obtain the license, influence the regulator, cultivate the prosecutor and let the law itself define who may compete. The mob, as the trope goes, “goes legitimate.” Northeast Oklahoma has a documented history that makes that question unusually difficult to dismiss. In the early 1970s, federal courts exposed an illegal gambling and protection conspiracy centered around the Grove-area club known as Mr. Yuk. items.title: WHEN EVERYBODY KNOWS EVERYBODY
items.summary: WHEN EVERYBODY KNOWS EVERYBODY There was a time when Americans spoke of the small town as though it were a kind of moral clearinghouse. Everybody knew everybody. A man could not get too far ahead of his reputation. The banker knew his father. The sheriff knew where he lived. The lawyer had gone to school with his brother. The judge had eaten supper in half the houses represented before his court. This familiarity was supposed to keep men honest. Sometimes it did. Sometimes it merely taught them how to get along. There is a difference. In a large city, public business is often impersonal to the point of absurdity. In a small town, it may be personal to the point of danger. The same names turn up again and again. The same lawyers practice before the same judges. The same contractors seek the same public work. The same officers testify in the same courts. The same civic leaders sit on the same boards, attend the same fundraisers, shake hands at the same dinners, and bury one another's parents. A stranger looking at the arrangement may see a web. items.title: The Record as a Condition of Review: Verbatim Reporting, Due Process, and Appellate Accountability in Oklahoma Courts
items.summary: The Record as a Condition of Review: Verbatim Reporting, Due Process, and Appellate Accountability in Oklahoma Courts A Juridical Analysis of 20 O.S. § 106.4, Oklahoma Appellate Doctrine, Electronic Recording, and the Limits of Narrative Reconstruction Current through August 25, 2026 Abstract An appellate court ordinarily reviews what the record demonstrates, not what a litigant later asserts occurred in the courtroom. That elementary principle gives court reporting a constitutional dimension that extends beyond administrative convenience. When judicial rulings, objections, argument, testimony, evidentiary exclusions, or findings are not preserved, an appellate court may be unable to determine whether error occurred. Oklahoma law addresses that danger unusually explicitly. Title 20, section 106.4 of the Oklahoma Statutes provides for full reporting of judicial proceedings by an assigned court reporter and declares that certain refusals to permit or require statements to be reported or transcribed constitute a denial of due process. items.title: The Marked Generation: Why Tattoos, Piercings, and Septum Rings Became Mainstream for American Women
items.summary: During the past two decades, tattoos, facial piercings, and especially septum rings have traveled from recognizable subcultural markers toward ordinary features of American female appearance. The change tells us something larger about individuality, friendship, commerce, technology, and the manner in which a culture teaches people what to find beautiful. Body modification has moved steadily from the cultural margins into ordinary American life, appearing today across professions, social classes, and everyday settings. What once belonged, at least in the public imagination, to relatively narrow social worlds has entered ordinary life. Tattoos appear on teachers, nurses, clerks, mothers, students, office workers, artists, and professionals. Nose piercings have become commonplace. Septum rings, once strongly associated with punk, alternative fashion, or deliberate unconventionality, now appear across a much wider range of ages and social settings. items.summary: Who Can Rule the Self? items.title: How Fats Waller’s Harmonic Architecture Translates to the Fretboard through Chromatic Barre-chord Slides, Pedal Tones, Walking Bass, Altered Dominants, and Economical Voice Leading
items.summary: Jazz Guitar • Voice Leading • Fats Waller • Harmonic Analysis How Fats Waller’s harmonic architecture translates to the fretboard through chromatic barre-chord slides, pedal tones, walking bass, altered dominants, and economical voice leading. Ain’t Misbehavin’ does not need to be reharmonized to become harmonically fascinating. Much of that sophistication is already embedded in the song. The diminished movement, secondary dominants, relative-minor excursions, and circle-of-fifths turnaround belong to the underlying architecture. What changes on guitar is how that architecture moves . In this arrangement, the original framework is filtered through a distinctly guitaristic vocabulary: full barre shapes slide by half step, bass notes move independently beneath stable upper voices, dominant chords acquire sixths, ninths, and thirteenths, and a tonic pedal can remain fixed while the rest of the chord descends chromatically above it. items.summary: Russian Lullaby From Irving Berlin to Jerry Garcia: A Guitarist’s Study of Descending Minor Harmony, Borrowed Chords, Dominant Chains, and Chromatic Improvisation Irving Berlin’s Russian Lullaby is an unusually rich example of what can happen when a popular song passes through several generations of musicians. Written in 1927, the composition moved from Tin Pan Alley into swing and jazz, then eventually into Jerry Garcia’s repertoire, where its harmony became fertile ground for lyrical guitar improvisation. For a guitarist, the Garcia-influenced version is especially revealing. The song contains a descending D-minor line cliché, a sudden opening into F major, the haunting borrowed-minor movement Bb → Bbm → F , a chain of dominant sevenths, and a final section that repeatedly circles the dominant before resolving home. The central lesson of Russian Lullaby: The chords may have names, but the deeper structure is often a collection of individual voices moving by half-step. 1. items.title: Caravan: A Jazz Manouche Guitarist’s Guide to the A7–Bb7 Vamp, Dominant Chains, Diminished Harmony, and Chromatic Improvisation
items.summary: Caravan in D Minor A Jazz Manouche Guitarist’s Guide to the A7–Bb7 Vamp, Dominant Chains, Diminished Harmony, and Chromatic Improvisation For guitarists, one of the most compelling ways to approach Duke Ellington and Juan Tizol’s Caravan is the D-minor Jazz Manouche treatment. Rather than simply holding a dominant chord until the melody finally reaches the tonic, this arrangement turns the dominant itself into a rhythmic and chromatic event. The central sound is an A7 dominant pedal , repeatedly disturbed by a chord or upper structure one semitone higher, Bb7 , before the accumulated tension finally collapses into Dm . Then the bridge begins moving: D7 → G7 → C7 → F7 In the version studied here, that dominant chain continues through an especially effective chromatic turn: F7 → E7 → A7 → Dm The result is a nearly perfect laboratory for a guitarist interested in dominant harmony, diminished chords, chromatic side-slipping, arpeggio-based improvisation, and the idea that tension becomes meaningful when its destination is clear. items.title: Shady Grove: From Appalachian Modal Song to Doc Watson, Jerry Garcia, and David Grisman
items.summary: Shady Grove From Appalachian Modal Song to Doc Watson, Jerry Garcia, and David Grisman Some songs invite harmonic sophistication by containing many chords. Shady Grove does almost the opposite. Its extraordinary power comes from how much melody, rhythm, ambiguity, and improvisation can grow from very little harmony. At its most elemental, the tune can live almost entirely between: Dm ↔ C Two chords. Yet within that small field we can hear Appalachian old-time music, modal fiddle language, flatpicked guitar, bluegrass vocabulary, blues inflection, Garcia's spacious melodic improvisation, and David Grisman's highly conversational acoustic approach. items.title: Minor Swing: A Guitarist’s Harmonic Map to Django Reinhardt’s Masterpiece
items.summary: Minor Swing , 1937 A Guitarist’s Harmonic Map to Django Reinhardt’s Masterpiece Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli’s Minor Swing is one of those rare compositions whose apparent simplicity conceals an enormous harmonic world. The underlying form is only sixteen bars long. Its principal harmony revolves around A minor, D minor, and E7. Yet those few chords support chromaticism, diminished harmony, minor-sixth colors, tritone substitution, altered dominant sounds, and virtually the entire twelve-note chromatic vocabulary when handled with convincing voice leading. That is the central lesson of Minor Swing : improvisation is not primarily a question of finding a scale containing only “correct” notes. It is a question of knowing where the harmony is going . items.summary: Wyandotte Nation joins regional wildlife reciprocity compact Agreement creates shared licensing, harvest reporting and enforcement framework, but does not automatically open private or tribal land. By Miami News-Digest MIAMI, Okla. — The Wyandotte Nation has joined other northeastern Oklahoma tribal nations in a new wildlife reciprocity agreement intended to expand hunting, fishing, trapping and conservation cooperation across participating tribal jurisdictions. Leaders signed the agreement Aug. 4 during an Inter-Tribal Council event, according to announcements from the Wyandotte Nation and Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma. Wyandotte regulations identify Lankford as the Nation’s wildlife representative. A conversation with artist and songwriter Sean Keith. Built around the progression Fmaj7 to E minor, A minor to E minor, and F to G to A minor, “If You Won’t, Then I Will” moves from vulnerability and confinement toward purpose, faith, and moral agency. Its images are dramatic, but its central declaration is restrained: another person may define the burden, but that person does not possess final authority over what the burden produces. items.title: Accountability Without Capacity: Public Records in Crisis
items.summary: Public transparency depends on frontline employees who must process records requests, protect confidential information, answer media inquiries, and navigate complex disclosure laws. Yet many government agencies assign this legally sensitive work to undertrained and overextended general staff, creating delays, over-redaction, burnout, and declining public trust. Accountability Without Capacity: Why Transparency Systems Break at the Front Line Freedom-of-information administration is frequently treated as clerical work when it is actually a hybrid of legal analysis, records management, digital forensics, privacy protection, project management, and public communication. The resulting failures are therefore better understood as organizational-design failures than as individual incompetence. The scale of the work is substantial. Federal agencies received approximately 1.71 million FOIA requests in fiscal year 2025 and processed approximately 1.64 million. Government-wide FOIA administration used about 4,823 full-time-equivalent staff and cost an estimated $661 million, including roughly $51 million associated with litigation. items.title: The Structural and Cinematic Function of the One Ring as an Instrument of Providence
items.summary: The Structural and Cinematic Function of the One Ring as an Instrument of Providence Subverting Power through the Lens of Grace: The One Ring, Cinematic Providence, and the Refinement of the Hero in Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings By Sean K. Gray Abstract Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings trilogy employs the visual scale and narrative momentum of the Hollywood epic while quietly overturning the epic's customary account of victory. Its armies, kings, fortresses, and cavalry charges appear to locate historical agency in organized power, yet the decisive action belongs to two hobbits whose journey progressively deprives them of physical strength, social status, certainty, and control. This essay argues that Jackson constructs the One Ring as an anti-talisman: an object that promises mastery while exposing the bearer's dependence, hidden desires, and moral limitations. Through extreme close-ups, isolating compositions, subjective sound, distorted point of view, rhythmic crosscutting, and contrasts between microscopic suffering and macroscopic warfare, the trilogy makes the Ring a psychological mirror and a structural instrument within a providential narrative. items.summary: The Cloud Wall SaaS Architecture, Generative Artificial Intelligence, and the Transformation of Software Piracy Definitions for General Readers The definitions on this page are written at approximately a fifth-grade reading level. The article that follows uses the terms in their more technical sense. Algorithm. A set of steps that tells a computer how to solve a problem or complete a task. Application programming interface (API). A controlled doorway through which one computer program can ask another program to do something. For example, an app may use an API to ask an AI system to create an image. API key. A secret code that identifies a person, program, or company using an API. It is similar to a password and should not be shared. Authentication. The process of proving who you are. Entering a password or using a security code are forms of authentication. Authorization. The process of deciding what an authenticated person or program is allowed to do. Backend. The part of a computer service that runs on the company’s servers.
